This section of E Marginal Way is a busy principal arterial that is part of the National Highway System (NHS), is classified as a T-2 road for freight (second highest rating by WSDOT), carries bus routes, and has bicycle lanes.  The purpose of the project is to extend the life of the existing pavement structure by 10 to 20 years.

Overall, the project will include the following:

	Milling and overlaying the asphalt pavement, conducting base repairs, and sealing pavement cracks.
	Repairing and installing sidewalk, ADA curb ramps, curb bulbs, and signal loops.
	Installing a two-way buffered bike lane on the northeast side of E Marginal Way S from S River Street south to Corson Ave S
	Installing a multi-use path on the northeast side of E Marginal Way S from Corson Ave S south to the existing multi-use path that extends from the "Flume Property" south to 16th Avenue S (the Flume Property is roughly due north of Slip 4 of the Duwamish Waterway)
	Restriping the resurfaced road for traffic and rechannelizing portions of the road
	Installing street luminaires, and, at the Corson Avenue intersection, installing traffic signal strain poles.
	Removing or abandoning some inlets and catch basins and their connecting pipes and installing new inlets, catch basins and connecting pipes.
	Planting street trees.

The work within the shoreline zone will generally consist of milling and overlaying the asphalt pavement, conducting base repairs, sealing pavement cracks, and installing a 35 foot wood pole to which a street luminaire and cables will be attached.

properties.description:
***Need DAP ASSIGNMENT for parcel number 7129302620***

Hello,

This is an application to build a "Cottage Housing Development" on an empty parcel of land (7129302620). This parcel doesn't yet have an address. I have been instructed to say "Please assign address for vacant parcel 7129302620.". 

This is a "green" project that consists of 4 separate cottages and covered parking. This parcel is in an Environmentally Critical Area (Potential landslide/steep slope). While this parcel is mostly sloped there is a portion that is actually flat. There are homes higher up on the slope and a home that is adjacent to this parcel on the slope. 

The proposed structures are cohesive with the nature of the parcel. They are underground earth-sheltered structures with green roofs/living roofs. They are simple rectangle structures that are one story studios/one bedrooms. These structures are essentially retaining walls that double as dwellings. Meaning, they will essentially be basements that are nearly completely covered with soil/grass. These structures will be anchored by "heels" and "toes". It is important to note that theses structures do not result in impervious surfaces due to their nature.

The grass "roofs" function to soak up rain, however drainage would be added to pass rainfall to a Rainwise cistern -this parcel qualifies for that program.

The introduction of this Cottage housing development will stabilize the ground for neighboring parcels and will be an overall positive additional to the area. 

Very respectfully,

Austin Payne and Kyara Tabosa

properties.description:
This project was based on dealing with water runoff. We have an active landslide to our north and others nearby. We had a scare and hired engineers to design us a retaining wall, which came in at more than 450k. One of them told us our home could be red tagged. Long story short, we didn't do the 450k solider wall and decided to go with just replacing what was already in place but adding water control for rain water. We also added safety rails, and stairs to replace rotten stairs or unsafe stairs, or in the case of the concrete stairs (main) it was to replace the historic concrete path that came up to the house but was broken and uneven in places (unsafe). So thats about it. We worked on it for a long time, and now its safe for my small kids, now the water all comes into the system insted of coming down the hill onto my neighbors (such as Peter M) who had to spent 250K on a retaining wall because of a slide on HIS property a number of years ago, but before we moved here. So yes, drainage - all using gravity which all ends up in the same system. That system ends in a water vault. 

Lastly, we have spent a huge amount of money on replanting already - with native plants. We're not doing all it on our own, and have a steep stope professional who comes to help. We are removing invasive and toxic vegatation very slowly as we replace the root space with native plants. 

Lastly I will add that we didn't disturb the soils. We just worked with the topography and especially in the case of the concrete path, we just used the footprint that was already there. I have some of those photos.

properties.description:
During the summer of 2023, contact between vessels and the pier facility operated by Pacific Terminals, Inc, sustained significant structural damage to the pier structure rendering a portion of it unusable for business purposes. The impact damaged  two 14" fender piles, two HDPE chaffing plates and detached these pilings from the exisitng piling cap.

The damage has rendered approximately 20 lineal feet of the berth unusable for business. Repairs must be conducted as soon as possible to be included in the present fish window and minimize lost revenue. 

Pacific Terminals is proposing to replace the following items at the Terminal 7 dock due to damage from a recent vessel impact;
-Pull and replace two existing damaged 14" fender timber piles with 14" steel or UHMW/HDPE or similar poly-coated timber pile
- Pull and replace two HDPE chaffing plates on newly installed fender piles
-Reattach all replaced pilings to replaced piling caps with galvanized hardware

properties.description:
To remodel an existing house and add two modular buildings on site for use by Villa Comunitaria, Duwamish River Community Coalition, and Duwamish Valley Youth Corp.

The initial phase of the project will include the remodel of an existing house and addition of two modular buildings on the adjacent parcel. Site improvements at this initial phase include a parking lot with stormwater facilities and utility connections.  
The modular buildings will remain on the site for five years while the stakeholder coalition organizes fundraising. 
The subsequent phase will include the demolition of the existing house and removal of the modular buildings. This future design will be a 2-3 story multipurpose community services building, with a 3,000sf multipurpose room, and smaller parking lot.

properties.description:
The General Recycling of Washington (GRW) Habitat Restoration Project (Project) is planned to be constructed within GRW's facility located at 4260 West Marginal Way SW in Seattle, Washington, on the west bank of the Lower Duwamish River (LDR). Although the GRW facility spans three tax parcels, Parcel Nos. 7666703540, 7666703630, and 1824049018, construction of the proposed Project will predominantly occur on Parcel No. 7666703540, with a smaller portion in the northeastern corner of Parcel 7666703630, as shown in the Site Plan on Sheet 1 of 2.
 
The proposed Project is required by Consent Decree between GRW and the Natural Resource Trustees (Trustees) to settle Natural Resource Damage claims associated with historical contamination in the LDR linked to the GRW facility. The Trustees include the National Oceanic Atmosphere Administration, the Department of the Interior, the State of Washington through the Washington State Department of Ecology, the Suquamish Indian Tribe of the Port Madison Reservation, and the Muckleshoot Indian Tribe. The purpose of the Project is to construct a new habitat area specifically designed to support juvenile salmonids, aquatic habitat diversity, and ecosystem health. The proposed Project will be constructed on a total of 2.9-acres and will include a riparian buffer, vegetated marsh habitat, intertidal and subtidal habitat zones.  Approximately 1.5 acres of upland area will be converted to aquatic habitat, as shown in the Habitat Concept Plan on Sheet 2 of 2.

properties.description:
Cascade Public Media (CPM), a prominent local media organization, is embarking on an exciting venture as they relocate to their new headquarters located at 316 Broadway. This building was originally constructed by Childhaven, a school dedicated to nurturing young minds. The property is currently zoned as MR(M), which imposes certain restrictions on signage, particularly limiting them to a maximum height of 15 feet. However, with CPM's vision for the building, the team is keen to explore the possibility of obtaining a zoning variance that would enable the installation of a distinctive wall sign on the south-facing upper story of this impressive 5-story structure.

The decision to seek a zoning variance for signage is driven by the building's transformation into a commercial office space, complete with a first-floor event area. This shift in function and the building's importance within the community make it essential for CPM to align its signage with its new role effectively. To accomplish this, CPM is aiming to have its signage proposal reviewed under the NC3 sign code. The NC3 zoning classification is well-suited for properties in the surrounding area and has the flexibility needed to accommodate signage that complements the building's use as both a commercial office space and a venue for community events.

By pursuing this zoning variance and aligning their signage with the NC3 code, CPM demonstrates their commitment to both preserving the building's historical significance and adapting it to serve the evolving needs of the community. This move not only reflects CPM's dedication to their mission but also underscores their desire to create a welcoming and distinctive presence in the heart of the community while respecting the building's storied past.

properties.description:
I entered the following information on Marcy 19 and haven't received a response. Can you help? Royce Morrison 206-799-7386 

With real estate attorney assistance, we have reached a signed agreement with a neighbor to adjust a boundary line. The surveyed adjusted lot boundary will conform to the base of a rockery built in 1925. It is not straight, and the line will be described by a series of several straight line segments with all points described by the surveyor. The adjusted line will not come within 5 feet of either house, and the houses will remain at least 10 feet apart. 
The boundary to be adjusted runs through the SW and NW corners of our lot, and the NE and SE corners of the adjacent lot, and both of those areas are designated steep slope Environmentally Critical Areas (with no qualification except being steep - i.e., no history or stated risk of landslide).
Reading online, we see that a necessary Project Number will be given after a Preliminary Application Form is submitted. By telephone today, we learned that the PAF is no longer used, and all applications are done online. Please tell us how to proceed.
We saw on the old PAF form that max size of the site plan with PAF would be 11x17. From reading Tip 213B, we believe that the formal application may require an 18x24 survey map. Which should we ask the surveyor to provide, and in what format? 
Thank you!

properties.description:
*Application should be a shoreline EX, Proposal moved to 6968670-EX

Application in response to Shoreline Violations: 1054442-VI, 1055014-VI
Make demarcation on my property between the public Shore View Street End and my property adjacent to the South on the beach.  The SDOT will not fence or sign this street end, per Omar Akari.  Although he did say I could use temporary dune fencing.

Public used to use these 117 feet of beach (my 60', street end 20' and North adjacent 37' for partying wildly when both residences were inhabited by owners who had dementia for 5-10. Years.  The public still wants to trespass on my beach and tidelands, leaving behind dog waste, alcohol bottles, smoking paraphernalia, trash, condoms, etc. They also wish to launch small watercraft off and back onto my beach and tidelands, picnic, run in my sand yard after my dog and cat, yell at me when I very politely ask them to use the public area adjacent , or enjoy LIncoln Park just to the north 1/4 mile away.  People come to this tiny street end because  leave their dogs off leash, bc they see the private beach owners with their dogs.

I need some demarcation of my property.  I prefer as high a fence as you permit, to keep public from staring in my yard, yelling at me & my dog and cat.  Some public are violent.

***. I need the Shoreline Permit Exemption for Dune fencing, or driftwood fence perpendicular to the water on my private property within the allowable feet from the concrete bulkhead. It's a small, very low impact tiny project.

When the public gets aggressive and violent, is when I put up the bamboo higher fencing, to protect myself and my animals from them, and to keep my dry and wet sand sanitary.  It also protects the public's health and safety be containing them to their area, where they can see the trash and live with it, or pick it up.  

Technically, as I understand it this is a Shore View only Street End.  Public is not to access the water except during high tide, and not to infringe on the private dry and wet sand private property here.  I am okay with them walking straight down to the water's edge, and walking - keep moving along the shoreline.  They are not entitled to this, but as long as they comply and my property line is clearly marked, I can give this.

The City should be responsible for protecting both the public and the private citizens who pay big taxes to live here.

properties.description:
The Argosy float replacement project is intended to address the maintenance needs of a small existing float at Seattle's Pier 54, which has reached the end of its useful life. This float provides one of two downtown boarding locations for Argosy, making it a key component of Argosy's commercial tour operation. The float is also used for short-term moorage of maintenance and assist vessels. An in-kind replacement is needed; refer to the attached photographs of the existing, deteriorating float.
 
The project proposes to remove the existing float in its entirety. The float will be detached from its support piles and disposed of off-site. Thereafter, a prefabricated float will be delivered to the site via barge or tug and will be positioned within the same footprint as the previous float. The existing structure will be replaced with a new float constructed from standard, non-toxic materials, which, unlike in the present structure, will prevent continued deterioration.

Given the need for the float to support high load capacity during loading and unloading of passengers and cargo, and to ensure stability for public use in a wave-influenced environment, a complete subsurface floatation system is necessary. This results in 17% functional open space in this site's deepwater environment; this is the maximum functional open space that can be provided given the small size of the float and the safety and environmental conditions that influence final design.  
 
The float will connect to the six existing steel piles via five-sided pile hoops. Pile hoops will be connected by hand from a standing position on the new float or via a small support vessel accessing the pile hoops from 
beneath Pier 54.  
 
This project will occur overwater and will not require any in-water work. Removal of the existing float and installation of the new float is expected to be completed in 3 days or fewer.

properties.description:
The proposed project is to convert an existing 1 story, 5400sf mortuary building into the new home for the Rainier Valley Food Bank. 

The scope of work includes expanding and remodeling the existing building to allow food bank programs and operations to move in. Proposed spaces and alterations the design team is considering include: adding an interior or exterior walk-in cooler and a walk-in freezer; converting the existing lobby into a commercial kitchen with walk-up to-go window; adding a larger entry canopy; converting a large room into a grocery store-like distribution space; adding a small mezzanine; adding a loading dock; converting some existing parking spaces into a garden and waste enclosure; expand the building toward Rainier Ave by ~3900sf for additional office and staff support spaces.
There is also interest to activate and occupy the site with a temporary food village during the design, permitting, and construction process.

properties.description:
The proposed project will be a the installation of conveyance swales in the planting strip right-of-way that is adjacent to the address of 7551 8th Ave S.   
1. The intention is to continue with standing water remediations and hydrological improvements that began with Phase 1 (Permit #: SUCONSTX421616).  This will be done by regrading the slope of the parking strip so water flows into the planting strip where the conveyance swales will be installed.  This is ultimately designed so water doesn't collect on the street and pool at the parking lot of Gateway Park.     
2. The scope of work terminates within 200 feet of the shoreline and we will need a shoreline exemption for our work to proceed.
3. Parallel parking will be suspended for the duration of the project and new curbing will be installed between the street and the conveyance swales. 
4. Tree and vegetation installation is planned for within the swales. This will aid the area in air quality improvements, absorb the run-off water that the swales will be collecting, and improve the aesthetic qualities of Georgetown's only public access frontage to the Duwamish River.

properties.description:
Western Neon has been working in the Seattle area since 1985 to build, service, and maintain the Emerald City's illuminated signs. We are currently helping refurbish the infamous Pink Elephant Car Wash sign while also celebrating the unsung female artist and designer who created it. A private donor is interested in installing an edition of this iconic sign at the Northeast corner of 7th Ave and Blanchard Street. To ensure this sculpture is viewed as a work of art, we are requesting a MUP Variance for this under Conditions 3 and 5 and then apply for a City of Seattle Sign Permit and proceed. That said, please see below for information on how we classify this unique object and how we would identify the artist on an informational plaque adjacent to the installation:

Pink Elephant II

The Pink Elephant II is a refurbished sculptural monument celebrating the original sign sited at the intersection of Denny and Dexter Avenues in proximity to Highway 99. It combines an original sign shell with new glass, electrical components, internal structure, and hardware while incorporating a decorative base reminiscent of the first Pink Elephant designed by artist Beatrice Haverfield.

Neon and argon filled glass tubing, phosphorus powder, glass, aluminum, copper, patinated enamel over sheet metal, seven electromagnetic transformers, animator, GTO, carbon steel, stainless steel, hardware, 122" x 24" x 110", Seattle, 1956.

About the Artist: Beatrice Haverfield

Beatrice Haverfield (1913-1996) was an unparalleled artist, designer, and visionary who transformed the Seattle urban landscape. While her impact can be marked and remembered, her legacy is immeasurable. Beatrice was creative from an early age and honored her artistic talents while soaking up the rapidly changing Seattle skyline. From her first company with high school sweetheart Elden Fisler to her time with burgeoning company Campbell Neon, Beatrice was a unique and instrumental force. 

In her time, she created the infamous "Ivar's" sign on Pier 54, the futurist look of blue-collar mainstay "Chubby & Tubby's" as well as "The Dog House" and "Dick's Drive-In" and a multi-colored, show-stopping landmark for Cinerama. Never to rest on her laurels, Beatrice pulled out all the stops for her masterpiece, "The Pink Elephant." 

This one-of-a-kind monumental sculpture was more than a sign as it evoked an entire library of personal design moves. From characteristic script to industrial text, the "Pink Elephant" was a sublime mix of light, space, time, and commerce spinning above one of the busiest intersections in the city it symbolized - a city always on the way up, glittering against the ocean, mountains, and trees day and night.

Please let me know if you have any questions and we look forward to working with you to establish the next steps as well as a realistic pre-construction, fabrication, and installation schedule based on a variance approval and permitting.

properties.description: Sound Transit plans, builds, and operates regional transit systems and services to improve mobility in urban areas of King, Pierce and Snohomish counties.  The voter approved ST3 Plan included Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) projects as part of ST's high-capacity transit (HCT) service to be designed for fast and reliable service, including frequent arrivals and departures.  The SR 522/NE 145th Street BRT project (the Project) will run along NE 145th Street and SR 522 from the Shoreline South/148th Station to Bothell and terminating at the planned SR 522/I-405 Transit Hub.  Figure A-1 shows the proposed project including the BRT route, station locations, and parking garage locations and transit priority treatments. The Shoreline segment is shown in green.  Service will run every 10 minutes all day between Seattle/Shoreline and Bothell.    Riders will be able transfer to Link Light Rail at the Shoreline South/NE 148th Link light rail Station, to the I-405 BRT in Bothell, and to King County Metro and Community Transit bus service.

properties.description:
"The goal of this process is to build a single family house on this lot maximizing the square footage to due the very expensive costs to build (given that the entire area is a steep slope with potential landslides).  We would also like to align ourselves with Seattle's Master Design Plans to enhance the Single Family Neighborhoods by adding 2 ADUs to the project.
The ECA Variance request is here because the property has Type IV Ns wetlands less than 1000 sq ft, riparian corridor, steep slopes, and shoreline districts.  there is a stormwater culvert which runs through the middle of this steeply sloped property, noted as a non fish-bearing Riparian Corridor, and in minimizing the riparian management area to 50 feet and reducing the yards by up to 25%, I would not be able to build a house that would meet reasonable use standards for the cost to build while staying outside of the steep slope buffers and staying outside of the Shoreline District.  And given that an ECA Variance is less environmentally impactful than a Shoreline Variance, we want to stay away from modifications that would trigger a Shoreline Variance.  Instead, we will move the house and ADUs away from the Shoreline District and toward the wetlands and the steeper slopes.  Given the Wetlands are Type IV Ns < 1000 sq ft, we plan to fill those in and mitigate them elsewhere on the property.
In addition, the property should qualify for a Shoreline Exemption according the the SMC codes that I have read, thus I will by applying for this as well."

"The goal of this process is to build a single family house on this lot maximizing the square footage to due the very expensive costs to build (given that the entire area is a steep slope with potential landslides).  We would also like to align ourselves with Seattle's Master Design Plans to enhance the Single Family Neighborhoods by adding 2 ADUs to the project.
The ECA Variance request is here because the property has Type IV Ns wetlands less than 1000 sq ft, riparian corridor, steep slopes, and shoreline districts.  there is a stormwater culvert which runs through the middle of this steeply sloped property, noted as a non fish-bearing Riparian Corridor, and in minimizing the riparian management area to 50 feet and reducing the yards by up to 25%, I would not be able to build a house that would meet reasonable use standards for the cost to build while staying outside of the steep slope buffers and staying outside of the Shoreline District.  And given that an ECA Variance is less environmentally impactful than a Shoreline Variance, we want to stay away from modifications that would trigger a Shoreline Variance.  Instead, we will move the house and ADUs away from the Shoreline District and toward the wetlands and the steeper slopes.  Given the Wetlands are Type IV Ns < 1000 sq ft, we plan to fill those in and mitigate them elsewhere on the property.
In addition, the property should qualify for a Shoreline Exemption according the the SMC codes that I have read, thus I will by applying for this as well.". 4130 NE 142ND ST

properties.description:
The proposed Pier 1 demolition and replacement activities include:

(1)Demolition of the existing Pier 1 timber and concrete structure.
(2)Installation of a commercial grade pier and an adjacent marina facility within the previous pier footprint. Activity is anticipated to include installation of a sheet pile wall within a portion of the aquatic habitat below the existing pier. Filling activities will occur behind the sheet pile wall to support installation of the new pier and marina facility.
(3)

Restoration of the existing shoreline revetment adjacent to the new pier and marina.
(4)Shoreline excavation to create area of gravel beach to compensate for unavoidable aquatic habitat impacts.






The existing pier consists of approximately 1,900 creosote piles and is significantly deteriorated with only a perimeter concrete apron that is in any measure of serviceable use. Replacement of the pier is needed to maintain the industrial/commercial marine use of the pier.

Based on soil and groundwater investigations, it is reported that upland soil, composed predominately of fill materials, is contaminated with metals and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs).

Restoration of the existing shoreline revetment is needed to prevent further erosion of the shoreline, and will assist in containing contaminated upland soils onsite.

Fill activities proposed below a portion of the existing pier's footprint, will partially utilize upland contaminated soils and suspected contaminated sediment (to the extent practicable) that will be disturbed during the course of  pier demolition and replacement activities and shoreline restoration. A sheet pile wall is proposed waterward of the area of fill to provide containment of the upland soil and dewatered sediment and protect the new pier structure. The new retaining wall feature will be contiguous with adjacent proposed shoreline revetment.
